name: Eureka
one_liner: An LLM writes robot reward code, simulated RL scores it, and a text summary of training guides the next rewards.

loop.proposes: Reward-function code written by GPT-4 from the simulator's source code and a task description (16 candidates per iteration)
loop.judged_by: RL (PPO in Isaac Gym) trains a policy on each reward; a ground-truth fitness function scores it
loop.steers: The best reward and a text summary of each reward component during training go back into the prompt

headline_result: Across 29 open-source RL environments with 10 robot morphologies, in simulation, the abstract reports Eureka outperforming expert human-written rewards on 83% of tasks, with an average normalized improvement of 52%. It also used its rewards in a curriculum to get a simulated Shadow Hand to perform pen spinning.
caveat: Results are in simulation, with human reward baselines from the benchmark authors and a fixed fitness function. Searching costs 5 independent runs of 5 iterations with 16 samples each, many RL trainings per task.
beyond_harness_note: A physics simulator and RL training decide reward quality, and the product is a reward function that stays useful without the LLM.
algorithmic_authority: RL training in Isaac Gym with a ground-truth task fitness function

sources.title: Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding Large Language Models (ICLR 2024)

verification.notes: Read the arXiv abstract and the full PDF text. Confirmed: NVIDIA, UPenn, Caltech, UT Austin; ICLR 2024; 5 iterations, K=16 samples per iteration, 5 independent runs per environment; gpt-4-0314; reward reflection; 83% and 52% from the abstract; 29 environments (9 Isaac plus 20 Dexterity). Eureka matches or exceeds humans on all Isaac tasks and 15 of 20 Dexterity tasks. Added from the robotics-gap list, not in the report's 27 entries. Review 2026-11-03: headline numbers re-checked against the source.
